title: A verifiable citizen identity is modeled with explicit types
excerpts: The book shows that a contract can organize types, ledger, witnesses, and circuits inside the same unit.
A verifiable identity stops being abstract once the contract models it with a well-defined type.

title: How the citizen registry is stored in ledger
excerpts: Verifiable identities can be stored in a ledger `Map` so the contract can reference them later.
The book example uses an additional counter to track registry-related state.

export ledger registry: Map<Bytes<32>, Citizen>;
export ledger count: Counter;

title: How registration becomes a contract operation
excerpts: The book shows an exported circuit with typed arguments used to register data in the contract.
That circuit becomes the entry point that executes the registration mission.

codeBlocks.title: Circuit adapted to citizen enrollment

title: A registry is an operational `Map`, not just a declaration
excerpts: `Map<key_type, value_type>` is an unbounded set of mappings between key values and value values.
The book defines built-in operations so the registry can be operated directly instead of through parallel structures.

title: The real `Map` operations
excerpts: `insert(key, value): []` updates the Map to include a new value at a given key.
`lookup(key): value_type`, `member(key): Boolean`, and `size(): Uint<64>` complete the essential registry operations.

codeBlocks.title: Book signatures
codeBlocks.code:
insert(key: key_type, value: value_type): []
lookup(key: key_type): value_type
member(key: key_type): Boolean
size(): Uint<64>

title: How to validate an insertion before registration
excerpts: `member(key)` returns a `Boolean` telling you whether a key is already contained in the Map.
`insert(key, value)` adds or updates the registry entry for that key.

title: How to audit and query the registry
excerpts: `lookup(key)` retrieves the value for a key and may return another ADT.
`size()` returns the number of entries in the Map so the registry can be measured without mutating it.

codeBlocks.title: Lookup and count
codeBlocks.code:
const citizen = registry.lookup(citizenKey);
const total = registry.size();

excerpts: The book shows that named fields are recommended for clarity.
That pattern prevents confusion about which value belongs in each identity field.

title: Named, positional, and mixed construction
excerpts: The book presents three ways to create a struct: named fields, positional fields, and mixed construction.
For identity missions, named fields should be preferred because they are easier to audit.

title: How to initialize an empty dossier
excerpts: `default<Player>` creates an instance with default values for every field.
That gives a safe baseline before the verifiable identity is fully populated.

title: Why the mission depends on circuits
excerpts: Circuits define the contract's business logic.
The compiler turns them into zero-knowledge circuits capable of generating and verifying proofs.

excerpts: A circuit declaration includes the name, parameters, and return type.
The exported variant uses the same syntax with the `export` keyword added.

title: `export` versus internal helper
excerpts: `export` makes the circuit callable from TypeScript.
Without `export`, the circuit is only available to other circuits inside the contract.

codeBlocks.title: Public and internal circuits

title: `[]` is mandatory when there is no return value
excerpts: The book emphasizes that circuits without a return value use `[]`, not `Void`.
That difference is both syntactic and semantic: `Void` will not compile.
